title: 114 pages and counting: a careful look at the AX-5 proof
snippet: Dr. Hannah Weiss on the state of machine-assisted verification of the AX-5 preprint: central lemmas are being checked, the Leipzig replication complements but does not replace formal proof, and the field is right to withhold judgement. “Extraordinary claims require extraordinary checking.”
body_markdown:
Days after the Kyoto Consensus statement gathered some two hundred signatures behind the AX-5 framework, the 114-page preprint at the centre of the debate is receiving the scrutiny its authors asked for. Dr. Hannah Weiss, who leads a formal verification group at ETH Zurich, is among several researchers attempting machine-assisted verification of OF-2026-114, the preprint behind the “adaptive arithmetic” claims presented at the Kyoto conference on 2 October. Her position is unusual in a polarised news cycle: she neither disputes the announcement nor treats it as settled.

## A long proof under a bright light

Weiss’s group is transcribing the preprint’s central constructions into an interactive proof assistant, checking each inference mechanically. As of publication, the team has verified the statement of the core AX-5 model construction and a first cluster of supporting lemmas; the remaining auxiliary results — the bulk of the document’s length — are still being worked through. The group’s method is deliberately redundant: separate members formalise the same lemma independently, and the two transcriptions are compared before anything is marked as settled. She is emphatic that this pace is normal.

“The announcement was precise, and the authors have been careful — Miriam Adler’s plenary was a model of restraint,” she says. “But extraordinary claims require extraordinary checking, and one hundred fourteen pages is a lot of checking. Machine assistance does not make it instant; it makes it reliable.”

## What verification can and cannot settle

Weiss distinguishes between two questions that coverage has tended to merge: whether the derivations in OF-2026-114 are correct, and whether AX-5 matters. Formal verification speaks to the first. The “Leipzig replication” announced on 8 October — in which Dr. Sofia Lindqvist’s group at the Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in the Sciences independently rebuilt the framework’s constructions — is complementary: a computational reproduction rather than a completed formal proof.

“The replication tells us the construction is robust enough to rebuild independently,” she says. “It does not yet tell us the framework has earned the word ‘arithmetic.’ That argument is partly philosophical, and the critics’ memo circulating in the community — the one calling AX-5 ‘notation, not arithmetic’ — deserves a place in it. All three positions are live: proponents, critics, and the undecided with proof assistants.”

Weiss notes that the field’s institutions have so far behaved sensibly. The Clay Mathematics Institute declined to convene a prize-dispute panel; universities are studying the claims rather than announcing positions; and the preprint itself keeps classical arithmetic intact for low-load contexts, which bounds the practical stakes while the checking proceeds.

## The honest position

Asked whether she expects the verification to finish cleanly, Weiss declines to predict. Her working estimate is that the remaining lemmas occupy the group for weeks, not days, and she declines to attach a deadline to the outcome. Her group will publish its progress openly as lemmas are completed, and she expects other groups to do the same. The alternative — accepting or dismissing a 114-page argument on announcement-day instinct — is, in her view, the one clearly wrong move.

“If the result stands, we will want the verification more, not less,” she says. “If it does not stand, the verification will show us exactly where it fails. Either way, the work is worth doing slowly and in the open. Scepticism is not opposition; it is the form our confidence will eventually take.”
